title: Everyday mysticism
hook: Karl Rahner said the Christian of the future would be a mystic or nothing
tomorrow: For the life of the world

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thomas Merton: a monk who found the crowd at the end of the silence. Your line was contemplation is for all. Where did you find a quiet minute in a busy place? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-five.

Who counts as a mystic? Saints with visions. Hermits in caves. People who seem to float a little above the rest of us. Karl Rahner, a German Jesuit priest and theologian, gave a different answer. He's remembered for saying, in effect, that the Christian of the future will be a mystic, or will not be anything at all. That sounds like an impossibly high bar, until you hear what he meant by mystic. A new week starts here, and it starts in an ordinary place. Today, mysticism in the everyday.

For Rahner, a mystic isn't someone with visions. He means someone who has actually experienced God, not only heard about God secondhand. Faith that rests on custom alone, he thought, would struggle in a world where custom no longer carries people along. So where would ordinary people meet God? Rahner's answer is the surprising part. Not mainly in rare moments, but inside daily life. He wrote about moments like these. Keeping silent when you've been wronged and could defend yourself. Forgiving when no one will thank you for it. Doing what your conscience asks when no one will ever know. Staying faithful in a task that brings no reward and no feeling of glory. In moments like that, he said, a person may be touching the Spirit at work, even if it feels like nothing at all. The letter to the Colossians, speaking about ordinary household work, says something close: "And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men." If that's so, then the kitchen, the commute and the office aren't outside God. Rahner's name for this was a mysticism of everyday life. Not a ladder out of the ordinary. A way down into it. Other Christians have said it in their own words. Brother Lawrence, a Carmelite lay brother who worked in the kitchen, spoke of practicing the presence of God among the pots and pans. The vocabulary differs, and the direction is the same: the plain moment may be the place.
screen: `A MYSTIC: ONE WHO HAS EXPERIENCED GOD.`
`NOT A LADDER OUT, A WAY IN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find God in a daily moment. Settle, and breathe. Look back over the last day. Search for one ordinary moment that held something more: a time you held your tongue, a kindness nobody saw, a task you finished well with no one watching. Don't judge whether it counts. Just stay with it, and notice what was there. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for that moment. If you don't, simply let it be noticed. The bell holds the time.
Everyday mysticism. Karl Rahner's idea that God can be met inside daily life itself: in silence, in forgiveness, in faithfulness no one sees.
Your line: mystic in the ordinary. Today, do one right thing nobody will notice, and let that be enough. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Some Christians end the day by looking back for where God was present in ordinary events, a practice known in Jesuit spirituality as the examen; others speak of practicing the presence of God in daily work.

fork.setup: a coworker takes credit for your work in a meeting. you could set the record straight, loudly. no one would ever know if you let it go. what does Rahner point to?
options: defend yourself in front of everyone.
keep silent and forgive, with no one noticing.
fork.reveal: Rahner names moments like this, keeping silent when wronged and forgiving without thanks, as places a person may touch the Spirit, even when it feels like nothing.

original.note: Greek, Colossians 3:23: from the soul. the King James renders it "heartily": "whatsoever ye do, do it heartily."

notes: Rahner's 'mystic or nothing' line is paraphrased without quotation marks ('in effect'); English translations are copyrighted. Please confirm the source essay and that 'a mystic, or will not be anything at all' is a fair paraphrase.
The everyday examples (silent when wronged, forgiving without thanks, obeying conscience unseen, faithful without reward) paraphrase Rahner's 'Reflections on the Experience of Grace'; confirm.
'Faith that rests on custom alone ... would struggle in a world where custom no longer carries people along' paraphrases Rahner's reasoning around the remark; confirm.
Brother Lawrence described as 'a monastery cook' (he worked in the kitchen of a Carmelite house in Paris); confirm.
